lead: Deoxyarbutin (dA) is a synthetic derivative of arbutin that inhibits tyrosinase, the enzyme that drives melanin production, and has been developed as a topical skin-lightening agent for hyperpigmentation such as age spots, solar lentigines and melasma, and for an overall brighter, more even complexion [1][4]. It is used in serums and creams as an alternative to hydroquinone, the long-standing standard lightening agent, which has been associated with multiple side effects [11].

It was described in a 2005 paper as a reversible tyrosinase inhibitor with skin-lightening activity in a pigmented guinea pig model, with inhibition of mushroom tyrosinase stronger than hydroquinone or arbutin in vitro, and with a 12-week human clinical trial showing reduced overall skin lightness in light-skinned volunteers and improvement of solar lentigines in dark-skinned volunteers [1]. A 2021 double-blind randomized trial in 59 women compared a 2 percent deoxyarbutin serum with a 4 percent hydroquinone serum on healthy skin and found comparable depigmenting efficacy [11]. Laboratory work has also examined its stability, its breakdown to hydroquinone and how it behaves under UV light [2][6][8].

chain: Deoxyarbutin competes with tyrosine at the tyrosinase enzyme
Less melanin is produced by melanocytes
Dark spots fade and skin tone looks lighter and more even
angle.text: People apply deoxyarbutin serums or creams daily to fade dark spots and uneven pigment, often as an alternative to hydroquinone. In studies, lightening appears gradually over weeks and reverses after stopping.

infobox: Melanin returned to normal in cultured cells within five days of removal [5]; guinea pig lightening reversed within 8 weeks [1]

paras: Deoxyarbutin was designed by quantitative structure-activity methods, as a tetrahydropyranyl ether of hydroquinone [5]. A 2009 study describes synthesizing it by removing all hydroxyl groups from the glucose side chain of arbutin [2]. Arbutin itself is a glucoside of hydroquinone; according to Wikipedia's arbutin article, the beta form is the common one, alpha-arbutin is a more potent stereoisomer, and in the EU the Scientific Committee on Consumer Safety has set a 7 percent limit in facial creams with hydroquinone contamination kept below 1 ppm [15].

Deoxyarbutin is thermolabile in water, where it decomposes to hydroquinone. A 2011 study reported that water increased decomposition in cosmetic emulsions and that a polyol-in-silicone anhydrous emulsion delayed degradation at 25 and 45 degrees C [8]. Formulation research has also tested lipid-carrier systems for skin delivery [17].

Tyrosinase inhibitors of this type resemble the enzyme's substrate, tyrosine, and compete for the catalytic site; deoxyarbutin was designed on this premise [1]. A 2008 study reported that deoxyarbutin and its second-generation derivatives inhibit tyrosine hydroxylase and DOPA oxidase activities of tyrosinase in a dose-dependent way, at concentrations that retained 95 percent cell viability, and that the effect was completely reversible when removed. It found deoxyarbutin to be a more robust competitive inhibitor than hydroquinone [4]. Another study found that deoxyarbutin and derivatives reduced tyrosinase activity and melanin synthesis without inducing reactive oxygen species or apoptosis in the cells tested [9].

A 2022 comparison of tyrosinase inhibitors noted that reported results for kojic acid, arbutins and deoxyarbutin differ between articles, and examined these compounds against mushroom tyrosinase and cultured B16F10 cells [3].

The safety of hydroquinone and its derivatives as whitening agents has been described as controversial [2]. In a 2006 study in cultured cells, the concentration of deoxyarbutin that kept 95 percent of melanocytes viable was four times that of hydroquinone, and keratinocytes and fibroblasts were also less affected [5]. A 2009 study in cultured melanocytes found that cytotoxicity of hydroquinone and arbutin rose with UVA exposure while deoxyarbutin's did not, and concluded that deoxyarbutin could be an alternative [2].

A 2017 study reported that UVB-irradiated arbutin and deoxyarbutin, which can break down into hydroquinone under higher energy, showed strong cytotoxicity to human fibroblast cells, especially deoxyarbutin, and still suppressed melanin in mouse melanoma cells [6]. Wikipedia's hydroquinone article reports that the FDA said it could not rule out hydroquinone as a carcinogen and that the agency banned it in over-the-counter products in 2020 [16].

The 2005 paper reported a 12-week human trial in which topical deoxyarbutin significantly or slightly reduced overall skin lightness and improved solar lentigines in light-skinned and dark-skinned individuals respectively [1]. A 2006 paper reported that in a clinical trial deoxyarbutin faded pre-tanned skin significantly more than either hydroquinone or no treatment, and that deoxyarbutin lightened human skin xenografts gradually over eight weeks [5].

In a 2021 double-blind randomized controlled trial, 59 women applied either 2 percent deoxyarbutin serum or 4 percent hydroquinone serum, one on each arm, daily for 12 weeks. Chromameter and mexameter readings showed significant lightening in both groups and comparable efficacy, and no side effects were reported in either [11]. A separate 2020 randomized trial tested a different tyrosinase-inhibiting compound against 2 percent hydroquinone; it lists deoxyarbutin among preparations described as toxic to melanocytes [10]. A 2015 review discusses the rationale for hydroquinone alternatives in melasma [12].

A 2017 laboratory study found that deoxyarbutin inhibited viability of mouse B16F10 melanoma cells through a mitochondria-associated apoptotic pathway, in vitro and in vivo [13]. A 2024 study reported it induced senescence in glioblastoma cells through mitochondrial damage, independent of tyrosinase [14]. A 2022 animal study investigated deoxyarbutin in severe acute pancreatitis [7]. None of these concerns appearance.

name: Deoxyarbutin

card.summary: A synthetic arbutin derivative that blocks tyrosinase in lab and animal work; human trial data are thin.
card.note: Evidence is mostly in vitro and animal; one study examined UVB-irradiated deoxyarbutin cytotoxicity.

quick.overview:
Deoxyarbutin is a lab-made relative of arbutin studied as a skin-lightening ingredient for dark spots and uneven pigment.
It was reported in 2005 to lighten skin in guinea pigs and to inhibit tyrosinase more potently than hydroquinone in a test-tube assay. Published human trials are lacking.
quick.mechanism: It competes with tyrosine at tyrosinase, the enzyme that makes melanin, reducing melanin production; studies describe the inhibition as reversible.
quick.risks: Researchers have compared its safety with hydroquinone in cultured cells and examined cytotoxicity of UVB-irradiated forms. Regulatory status is not established.
